01 — ONE NEURON

A neuron keeps a running total.

A pulse nudges the voltage upward. The nudge fades. If the voltage crosses the threshold, the neuron emits a spike and resets. Your job is to predict whether the input pattern will get there.

Will this neuron fire?

Make a prediction before Run.

Ready. The simulation clock is stopped.

VOLTAGE TRACE · THRESHOLD −45 mV · ONE DOT = ONE SPIKE

ILLUSTRATIVE TEACHING MODEL · LIF-TEACHING-V1

What the model is doing

  • Excitatory input adds to a fading conductance.
  • The membrane drifts back toward rest.
  • Inhibitory input subtracts from the same running total.
  • Cross the threshold, emit one spike, then reset.

How it works

The model advances in fixed 0.1 ms steps. A render frame cannot make the neuron run faster or slower; it only redraws the state that the simulation clock has already produced.

v ← v + (vrest − v) · Δt / τm + gexc − ginh
if v ≥ vthreshold: spike; v ← vrest

Model & evidence

This is a deliberately small LIF teaching model. It shares the basic integrate, leak, threshold, reset, and refractory ideas used by the research-derived engines, but it is not a reconstruction of a fly neuron and its output is not a biological firing-rate claim.

The useful evidence is causal and local: with the same initial state, changing pulse spacing or inhibition changes the trace. That is a model result, not a fact about every neuron.

What to notice

Try one weak pulse, then four close pulses. Same input size. Different timing. Biology is annoyingly temporal.

01b — ONE SMALL CIRCUIT

Now remove a connection.

This four-node circuit is an illustration of how a relay and an inhibitory branch can change an output. It is not a recovered Drosophila circuit. Click a node to inspect its voltage, then disable inhibition and run the same input train.
